title: Informal volunteering is a major but undercounted layer of social infrastructure, shaped by care, resources, and place
source_unit: ILO-UNV, Informal volunteering: Trends and characteristics
geography: Comparative country contexts covered by the ILO-UNV global analysis of informal volunteering

denominator.unit: global volunteering activity frame in the ILO-UNV report

informal_share.unit: approximately percent of all volunteering accounted for by informal volunteering

definition.value: Unpaid services provided to non-family members person-to-person, outside formal organizational structures, sometimes through registered or unregistered groups

recognition_gap.value: Many people doing informal volunteering do not self-identify as volunteers

observations.method: ILO-UNV comparative analysis of informal volunteering patterns and characteristics across diverse country contexts, with attention to who participates, how, and under what conditions.
observations.uncertainty: The approximately 70 percent figure is a report-level global composition estimate; definitions, instruments, recall, and country coverage can differ, and unrecognized activity is especially vulnerable to measurement error.
observations.subgroup: People providing unpaid help outside their household, community groups, formal volunteer organizations, public agencies, and recipients of person-to-person support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal volunteering remains important and may provide training, safeguards, and durable coordination; informal activity can supplement rather than replace public or organizational provision.

variation_axes.value: Engagement varies by age, gender, education, income, disability status, urban or rural location, and country

gender_main_effect.value: Gender alone does not greatly determine engagement in volunteer work in the report's comparisons

intersectionality.value: Intersections among gender and other demographic characteristics materially shape volunteering patterns

observations.method: Comparative subgroup analysis that keeps demographic and socioeconomic characteristics distinct and examines their intersections rather than treating one average participation rate as universal.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies patterned differences but does not make every subgroup comparison a causal estimate or establish that one characteristic produces participation differences independent of care, resources, health, safety, or local opportunity.
observations.subgroup: Women and men, different age and education groups, people with different incomes or disabilities, and urban and rural residents.
observations.counterinterpretation: Observed differences can reflect measurement, opportunity, social norms, household composition, or the kinds of activity counted; higher participation is not automatically lower burden or greater agency.

observations.period: 2026 publication; unpaid care and gendered time

denominator.unit: informal-volunteering participation comparisons involving unpaid care

care_constraint.value: Engagement in unpaid care in the home strongly reduces women's engagement in informal volunteering

time_competition.value: Informal volunteering competes with care and other unpaid or paid obligations for available time

visibility.value: Counting informal volunteering alongside unpaid care can reveal hidden civic and social infrastructure burdens

observations.method: ILO-UNV interpretation of subgroup patterns linking informal volunteering to unpaid care, household conditions, and the availability of time.
observations.uncertainty: The report does not estimate a universal causal effect of care on volunteering or the reverse; time competition can coexist with reciprocity, necessity, social norms, and different definitions of care and volunteering.
observations.subgroup: People with substantial unpaid care responsibilities, especially women, households relying on informal support, and communities with limited formal services.
observations.counterinterpretation: Care networks can enable volunteering by creating reciprocal support, and volunteering may sometimes provide respite or resources; reduced participation is not itself proof of exclusion.

denominator.unit: informal-volunteering measurement and support policy frame

policy_use.value: Better recognition and measurement can guide more inclusive volunteer strategies, data collection, and community-based interventions

social_protection_link.value: Informal volunteering evidence is relevant to inclusion, social protection, and community-based development

institutional_boundary.value: Recognition should support informal networks without treating unpaid community effort as a substitute for decent work or public provision

observations.method: ILO-UNV synthesis translating comparative evidence into measurement, inclusion, social-protection, and community-development implications.
observations.uncertainty: The publication identifies policy and research routes but does not demonstrate that recognition, funding, or formalization will improve participation, trust, service quality, or wellbeing in every context.
observations.subgroup: Volunteer-involving organizations, public authorities, social-protection systems, community groups, unpaid helpers, and people receiving informal support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal recognition can bring resources and protection but may also add reporting burdens, bureaucratic control, or eligibility rules that weaken flexible reciprocal support.

related_sources.claim: Persistent DOI and publication metadata for the ILO-UNV report.
Complementary ILO social-protection context for the boundary between unpaid support, public provision, and climate-transition protection.

boundary: This record adds an informal-volunteering, civic-capacity, unpaid-care, and social-infrastructure route. It uses comparative published evidence, not respondent-level volunteering histories, causal estimates of care or volunteering, individual service outcomes, or proof that formal recognition improves community wellbeing.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official ILO publication page reviewed for report definition, approximately 70 percent composition, subgroup variation, gender intersections, unpaid-care constraint, policy audience, and measurement implications.
